headline: Beavertail Tog Chew Green Crabs While Sakonnet's Rips Run Thick with Blues
subhead: The ledges are holding fish on the slack, the rips are loaded with bluefish, and the breachways are still waiting on their September guests.
body_markdown:
The crabs are moving on the ledges right now, and that's the tell. Green crabs skittering in the cracks at Beavertail, peelers working the rockweed at Brenton Point — that's what's had the tog interested all week, even though most guys still think of tautog as an October fish. Mid-July tog isn't a numbers game down here, it's a precision game. You find the right crack on the right stage of tide, drop a half a green crab on 20-pound fluoro straight to a jig head, and you wait for that thump you can't confuse with anything else.

I've been working Beavertail on the last hour of the ebb into the first hour of slack, 18 to 25 feet, right off the point where the current stacks up against the granite. Two keeper tog Tuesday, one that went better than seven pounds, both on green crab fished tight to the rock, almost no scope on the line. The bite shuts off hard once the tide starts pushing again — that current runs too fast through there for anything but a sinker the size of a doorknob, and even then you're just plowing bottom. Brenton Reef's fishing similar, though it's a longer commute if you're on foot; better as a boat spot where you can hold position on the slack instead of fighting for a rock to stand on.

Sakonnet Point is where the week got interesting. The rips off the point have been stacked with bluefish — 3 to 6 pounds, blitzing on peanut bunker that's in numbers along that stretch of shoreline. Dawn and dusk both, but dawn's been more reliable, right as the tide starts to move out of the harbor and pushes bait through the rip lines off the rocks. Poppers and metal — Deadly Dicks, half-ounce, worked fast through the white water — have been drawing crushing strikes. Mixed into that blitz have been schoolie stripers up to 28 inches, with the occasional better fish holding just off the edge of the feed, picking off cripples instead of joining the chaos. If you want the bigger bass, hang back from the bluefish melee and work a bucktail — 1.5 ounce, white — along the seam where the current edge meets the slower water. That's classic bottom-bounce structure fishing, and it's produced a few bass in the low-30s off that stretch this week.

Second Beach has had its own version of the same story — bunker schools moving along the beach front, blues underneath them showing up in the wash on the outgoing, stripers mixed in but outnumbered. If you're surfcasting there, don't waste time on the sandbar itself; work the deeper cut where the beach breaks toward Sachuest Point. That's held fish consistently on falling light.

Down toward the breachways — Charlestown, Weekapaug — it's been a fluke week more than anything else. Water's clean, not gin clear but working fine, and the sand flats just inside the breachway mouths have given up decent numbers of fluke to 4 pounds on the last two hours of the incoming, when bait gets pushed up out of the channel onto the flats. White Gulp Swimming Mullet on 3/4-ounce bucktails, dragged slow, has been the go-to. Scup fishing has been steady but unspectacular around the breachway rocks and the Jamestown bridge pilings — squid strips and clam on light tackle, good for the cooler box and good for kids, nothing to write home about beyond that.

Watch Hill and Napatree are quieter right now than they'll be in six weeks. The reef off Watch Hill has scup and the occasional keeper tog for guys willing to anchor up and soak crab, but I haven't seen or heard of peanut bunker pushing hard into that breachway yet — no sign of albies, and it's too early to expect them. That first wave doesn't usually show at Napatree or the Weekapaug cut until deep in September, sometimes not until the bunker schools get squeezed by cooling water further up the coast. Anybody telling you albies are around this week in RI waters is either mistaken or fishing a different ocean. What I'd watch for instead, over the next month, is how thick those peanut schools get in the coves — that's the real leading indicator, and right now they're just starting to organize.

Looking ahead, the pattern holds if the wind stays out of the south-southwest and doesn't kick up too much groundswell on the ledges — tog fishing depends on being able to hold bottom on slack, and a two-foot swell on the rocks turns Beavertail into a bad idea fast. If conditions stay clean, I'd keep working the ledges on the tide change for tog, hit Sakonnet at first light for the blitz, and use the breachways for a reliable fluke box while we wait on the real fall run to build. Nothing wrong with a mixed bag week — that's July on this shore.
